content: Hydrocortisone is a medication that can be obtained with or without a prescription. Low-strength formulations, such as 0.5% or 1%, are available over the counter and are used to temporarily alleviate minor skin irritations, itching, and rashes caused by conditions like eczema, insect bites, poison ivy, poison oak, poison sumac, soaps, detergents, cosmetics, and jewelry. It is also used to relieve itching in the anal and rectal areas, as well as itching and irritation of the scalp. Additionally, hydrocortisone can be applied to reduce the discomfort associated with mouth sores. When prescribed by a doctor, hydrocortisone is used to manage symptoms such as itching, redness, dryness, crusting, scaling, inflammation, and discomfort caused by various skin conditions. It may also be prescribed to treat inflammation associated with ulcerative colitis or proctitis, as well as swelling and discomfort caused by hemorrhoids and other rectal issues. In some cases, hydrocortisone may be used for other purposes, so it is important to consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Hydrocortisone is available in various forms, including ointments, creams, lotions, liquids, gels, medicated cloth towelettes, and sprays for topical use. For rectal use, it is available as foams, suppositories, creams, ointments, and enemas. It is also available as a paste for use in the mouth. For skin conditions, hydrocortisone is typically applied one to four times daily. For mouth sores, it is usually applied two to three times daily after meals and at bedtime. If mouth sores do not begin to heal within seven days, you should contact your doctor. For colitis, hydrocortisone is generally used every night or twice daily (morning and night) for two to three weeks. While colitis symptoms may improve within three to five days, regular enema use may be required for two to three months. If colitis symptoms do not improve within three weeks, consult your doctor. For proctitis, hydrocortisone is typically used once or twice daily for two to three weeks, and then, if necessary, every other day until the condition improves. Symptoms of proctitis may improve within five to seven days. For hemorrhoids, hydrocortisone is usually applied twice daily (morning and night) for two to six days. Always follow the instructions on the label carefully and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Use hydrocortisone exactly as directed and do not use more or less of it or use it more frequently than prescribed. If you are using hydrocortisone without a prescription and your condition does not improve within seven days, stop using it and contact your doctor. If the treated area worsens or develops redness, swelling, or oozing of pus, call your doctor immediately. When applying hydrocortisone ointment, cream, lotion, liquid, or gel to the skin, thoroughly wash or soak the affected area before application unless doing so causes irritation. Apply a thin layer of the medication and rub it in gently. For use on the scalp, part the hair, apply a small amount of the medication to the affected area, and rub it in gently. Avoid washing or rubbing the area until the medication has dried. You may wash your hair as usual, but not immediately after applying the medication. When using the aerosol spray, shake the container well and hold it 3-6 inches away from the affected area. Spray for about two seconds to cover an area the size of your hand. Avoid inhaling the vapors and protect your eyes if spraying near your face. Prolonged use on the face, genital and rectal areas, or in skin creases and armpits should be avoided unless directed by your doctor. When using hydrocortisone on a child’s diaper area, avoid tight-fitting diapers or plastic pants, as these may increase side effects. Do not apply cosmetics or other skin products to the treated area without consulting your doctor. If your doctor instructs you to wrap or bandage the treated area, follow these steps: 1. Wash or soak the area thoroughly. 2. While the skin is still moist, gently rub the medication into the affected area. 3. Cover the area with plastic wrap (e.g., Saran Wrap) and secure it with gauze, elastic bandages, or adhesive tape on the surrounding normal skin. Alternatively, plastic gloves, bags, or a shower cap may be used for hands, feet, or the scalp, respectively. 4. If the area is moist, leave the edges partially unsealed or puncture the wrap to allow excess moisture to escape. 5. Leave the plastic wrap in place for the duration specified by your doctor, typically no more than 12 hours per day. 6. Cleanse the skin and reapply the medication each time a new plastic wrap is applied. For rectal cream or ointment, apply it externally to the anal area. Some nonprescription creams may be used on the genital and anal areas; always read the product label carefully. When using a hydrocortisone enema, follow the provided instructions. Lie on your left side while administering the enema and remain in this position for 30 minutes afterward. Try to retain the enema for at least one hour, preferably overnight. Rectal foam also comes with specific instructions and should be applied using the provided applicator. Do not insert any part of the container into the rectum. After use, disassemble the applicator and clean it thoroughly with warm water. To insert a rectal suppository, follow these steps: 1. Remove the wrapper. If the suppository is too soft, chill it in the refrigerator for 30 minutes or run cold water over it before removing the foil wrapper. 2. Moisten the tip of the suppository with water. 3. Lie on your left side and raise your right knee to your chest (left-handed individuals should lie on their right side and raise their left knee). 4. Insert the suppository into the rectum using your finger (approximately ½ to 1 inch for infants and children, and 1 inch for adults). Hold it in place for a few moments. 5. Remain lying down for 15 minutes. Then, stand up, wash your hands thoroughly, and resume your normal activities. Be aware that some hydrocortisone suppositories may stain fabric, so take precautions as needed. Before using hydrocortisone, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to hydrocortisone or any other medications. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are taking, including cancer chemotherapy agents, other topical medications, and vitamins. Notify your doctor if you have an infection or a history of diabetes, glaucoma, circulation disorders, or immune disorders. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while using hydrocortisone, contact your doctor immediately. Do not use hydrocortisone on children under two years of age without consulting a doctor. If you miss a dose, apply it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not apply a double dose to make up for a missed one. Hydrocortisone may cause side effects. Minor side effects include drying or cracking of the skin, acne, itching, burning, and changes in skin color. If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your doctor. Severe side effects include a severe skin rash, difficulty breathing or swallowing, wheezing, or signs of a skin infection (redness, swelling, or oozing of pus). If you experience any severe side effects, contact your doctor immediately. Serious side effects can also be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store hydrocortisone in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Follow the storage instructions on the package. Dispose of outdated or unused medication properly by consulting your pharmacist. Keep all appointments with your doctor and do not share your medication with others. If you have questions about refilling your prescription, consult your pharmacist.
